description: 6 first-semester CS students at PUCMM, Santiago DR — no coders yet, using Claude/AI tools transparently. Challenge: Field Shift, Adapting Farms with NASA Data — Cibao valley's agricultural heart.
summary: When irrigation water runs short, Dominican rice farmers are told when not to plant rice, but nobody tells them what they can plant instead. GroundTruth Cibao is a free, bilingual web tool that answers that question with NASA data. A farmer answers six questions (zone, the crops they already grow, planting month and land, soil, the water they were allocated, and their priority) and gets a planting plan built only from crops they grow: how much land their water covers, a two-cycle rotation, and the risks. Irrigation needs come from 25 years of NASA POWER daily climate (2001–2025) processed with the FAO-56 method for 14 Dominican rice zones, shown on a real 3D relief from NASA SRTM elevation. It works on a phone and offline. A world prototype applies the same method to any country with the NASA POWER climatology. It is a support tool that still needs validation by agronomists, and it does not promise profits.
details:
What it does

In the Cibao, the North region produces 91.5% of the Dominican Republic's rice and 99.5% of it is irrigated. In dry years the authorities restrict rice (in 2019 INDRHI banned winter rice in Tavera, Monción, Mao and Montecristi), but farmers are left without an answer to "then what do I plant?". Our tool gives that answer, farm by farm.

How it works

1. The farmer picks their zone on a map of the 14 rice zones and sees its real 3D relief (NASA SRTM elevation) with rivers and dams.

2. They answer six questions: the crops they already grow, planting month and land (tareas or hectares), soil, the share of irrigation water they were allocated, and their priority (water, soil or income).

3. The tool computes the irrigation each crop needs in that zone and month, in a typical and a dry year, from 25 years of NASA POWER daily data (2001–2025) with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method and FAO crop coefficients.

4. The main plan uses only crops the farmer already grows and shows how much land the water covers, the water left over, the nitrogen a legume adds and a two-cycle rotation. Four engine strategies (rice only, rice + legume, rotation to sell, green manure) are shown as other options, with evidence and risks.

5. A map shows NASA POWER layers (water shortfall, soil moisture, heat), a MODIS satellite photo, and a water calculator for 31 crops.

6. World prototype: a NASA Blue Marble globe; for any country, provinces from geoBoundaries, its main crops from FAOSTAT, the NASA POWER climatology at each province centre, the same questionnaire, plan and rotation, and a country map with NASA POWER values per province.

Benefits and intended impact

It turns NASA climate data into a decision a farmer can act on before planting: keep as much land producing as the water allows, with crops they know how to sell, instead of leaving it idle. It speaks Spanish and English, works on a phone and offline (PWA), and lets a farmer print, share or save a one-page plan.

Tools

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no external libraries (it runs offline), Python 3.9 for the data pipeline and the rotation engine, and GitHub Pages for hosting.

Trust and limits

The web calculation and the Python engine match on 54,358 values across 609 scenarios with zero differences. We say what we do not know: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, crop values from FAO tables must be validated by a Dominican agronomist, we use no prices so we promise no profits, and the world version is a prototype (average year only, no country-level validation). Every figure on the page links to its source.

What makes it creative

It does not predict the water: the farmer enters what they were allocated, and NASA data answers what fits in it. The plan respects what the farmer already grows instead of telling them to switch to unfamiliar crops.
